Lemma 37.44.1. Let f:X→S$f : X \to S$ be a morphism of schemes. The following are equivalent:

  1. f$f$ is finite,

  2. f$f$ is proper with finite fibres,

  3. f$f$ is proper and locally quasi-finite,

  4. f$f$ is universally closed, separated, locally of finite type and has finite fibres.

Proof. We have (1) implies (2) by Morphisms, Lemmas 29.45.11, 29.21.10, and 29.45.10. We have (2) implies (3) by Morphisms, Lemma 29.21.7. We have (3) implies (4) by the definition of proper morphisms and Morphisms, Lemmas 29.21.9 and 29.21.10.

Assume (4). Pick s∈S$s \in S$. By Morphisms, Lemma 29.21.7 we see that all the finitely many points of X s$X_ s$ are isolated in X s$X_ s$. Choose an elementary étale neighbourhood (U,u)→(S,s)$(U, u) \to (S, s)$ and decomposition X U=V⨿W$X_ U = V \amalg W$ as in Lemma 37.41.6. Note that W u=∅$W_ u = \emptyset $ because all points of X s$X_ s$ are isolated. Since f$f$ is universally closed we see that the image of W$W$ in U$U$ is a closed set not containing u$u$. After shrinking U$U$ we may assume that W=∅$W = \emptyset $. In other words we see that X U=V$X_ U = V$ is finite over U$U$. Since s∈S$s \in S$ was arbitrary this means there exists a family {U i→S}$\{ U_ i \to S\} $ of étale morphisms whose images cover S$S$ such that the base changes X U i→U i$X_{U_ i} \to U_ i$ are finite. Note that {U i→S}$\{ U_ i \to S\} $ is an étale covering, see Topologies, Definition 34.4.1. Hence it is an fpqc covering, see Topologies, Lemma 34.9.7. Hence we conclude f$f$ is finite by Descent, Lemma 35.23.25. □$\square$

## 37.44 Applications of Zariski's Main Theorem, I

A first application is the characterization of finite morphisms as proper morphisms with finite fibres.

Lemma 37.44.1. Let f:X→S$f : X \to S$ be a morphism of schemes. The following are equivalent:

  1. f$f$ is finite,

  2. f$f$ is proper with finite fibres,

  3. f$f$ is proper and locally quasi-finite,

  4. f$f$ is universally closed, separated, locally of finite type and has finite fibres.

Proof. We have (1) implies (2) by Morphisms, Lemmas 29.45.11, 29.21.10, and 29.45.10. We have (2) implies (3) by Morphisms, Lemma 29.21.7. We have (3) implies (4) by the definition of proper morphisms and Morphisms, Lemmas 29.21.9 and 29.21.10.

Assume (4). Pick s∈S$s \in S$. By Morphisms, Lemma 29.21.7 we see that all the finitely many points of X s$X_ s$ are isolated in X s$X_ s$. Choose an elementary étale neighbourhood (U,u)→(S,s)$(U, u) \to (S, s)$ and decomposition X U=V⨿W$X_ U = V \amalg W$ as in Lemma 37.41.6. Note that W u=∅$W_ u = \emptyset $ because all points of X s$X_ s$ are isolated. Since f$f$ is universally closed we see that the image of W$W$ in U$U$ is a closed set not containing u$u$. After shrinking U$U$ we may assume that W=∅$W = \emptyset $. In other words we see that X U=V$X_ U = V$ is finite over U$U$. Since s∈S$s \in S$ was arbitrary this means there exists a family {U i→S}$\{ U_ i \to S\} $ of étale morphisms whose images cover S$S$ such that the base changes X U i→U i$X_{U_ i} \to U_ i$ are finite. Note that {U i→S}$\{ U_ i \to S\} $ is an étale covering, see Topologies, Definition 34.4.1. Hence it is an fpqc covering, see Topologies, Lemma 34.9.7. Hence we conclude f$f$ is finite by Descent, Lemma 35.23.25. □$\square$

As a consequence we have the following useful results.

Lemma 37.44.2. Let f:X→S$f : X \to S$ be a morphism of schemes. Let s∈S$s \in S$. Assume that f$f$ is proper and f−1({s})$f^{-1}(\{ s\} )$ is a finite set. Then there exists an open neighbourhood V⊂S$V \subset S$ of s$s$ such that f|f−1(V):f−1(V)→V$f|_{f^{-1}(V)} : f^{-1}(V) \to V$ is finite.

Proof. The morphism f$f$ is quasi-finite at all the points of f−1({s})$f^{-1}(\{ s\} )$ by Morphisms, Lemma 29.21.7. By Morphisms, Lemma 29.57.2 the set of points at which f$f$ is quasi-finite is an open U⊂X$U \subset X$. Let Z=X∖U$Z = X \setminus U$. Then s∉f(Z)$s \not\in f(Z)$. Since f$f$ is proper the set f(Z)⊂S$f(Z) \subset S$ is closed. Choose any open neighbourhood V⊂S$V \subset S$ of s$s$ with f(Z)∩V=∅$f(Z) \cap V = \emptyset $. Then f−1(V)→V$f^{-1}(V) \to V$ is locally quasi-finite and proper. Hence it is quasi-finite (Morphisms, Lemma 29.21.9), hence has finite fibres (Morphisms, Lemma 29.21.10), hence is finite by Lemma 37.44.1. □$\square$

Lemma 37.44.3. Consider a commutative diagram of schemes

X h f Y g S

$$  \xymatrix{ X \ar[rr]_ h \ar[rd]_ f &  &  Y \ar[ld]^ g \\  &  S }  $$

Let s∈S$s \in S$. Assume

  1. X→S$X \to S$ is a proper morphism,

  2. Y→S$Y \to S$ is separated and locally of finite type, and

  3. the image of X s→Y s$X_ s \to Y_ s$ is finite.

Then there is an open subspace U⊂S$U \subset S$ containing s$s$ such that X U→Y U$X_ U \to Y_ U$ factors through a closed subscheme Z⊂Y U$Z \subset Y_ U$ finite over U$U$.

Proof. Let Z⊂Y$Z \subset Y$ be the scheme theoretic image of h$h$, see Morphisms, Section 29.6. By Morphisms, Lemma 29.42.10 the morphism X→Z$X \to Z$ is surjective and Z→S$Z \to S$ is proper. Thus X s→Z s$X_ s \to Z_ s$ is surjective. We see that either (3) implies Z s$Z_ s$ is finite. Hence Z→S$Z \to S$ is finite in an open neighbourhood of s$s$ by Lemma 37.44.2. □$\square$

Lemma 37.45.2. Let $f : Y \to X$ be a quasi-finite morphism. There exists a dense open $U \subset X$ such that $f|_{f^{-1}(U)} : f^{-1}(U) \to U$ is finite.

Proof. If $U_ i \subset X$, $i \in I$ is a collection of opens such that the restrictions $f|_{f^{-1}(U_ i)} : f^{-1}(U_ i) \to U_ i$ are finite, then with $U = \bigcup U_ i$ the restriction $f|_{f^{-1}(U)} : f^{-1}(U) \to U$ is finite, see Morphisms, Lemma 29.45.3. Thus the problem is local on $X$ and we may assume that $X$ is affine.

Assume $X$ is affine. Write $Y = \bigcup _{j = 1, \ldots , m} V_ j$ with $V_ j$ affine. This is possible since $f$ is quasi-finite and hence in particular quasi-compact. Each $V_ j \to X$ is quasi-finite and separated. Let $\eta \in X$ be a generic point of an irreducible component of $X$. We see from Morphisms, Lemmas 29.21.10 and 29.52.1 that there exists an open neighbourhood $\eta \in U_\eta $ such that $f^{-1}(U_\eta ) \cap V_ j \to U_\eta $ is finite. Thus $U = X \setminus T$ is a dense open subset of $X$. We claim that $f|_{f^{-1}(U)} : f^{-1}(U) \to U$ is finite. To see this let $U' \subset U$ be an affine open. Set $Y' = f^{-1}(U') = U' \times _ X Y$, $V_ j' = Y' \cap V_ j = U' \times _ X V_ j$. Consider the restriction

\[ f' = f|_{Y'} : Y' \longrightarrow U' \]

of $f$. This morphism now has the property that $Y' = \bigcup _{j = 1, \ldots , m} V'_ j$ is an affine open covering, each $V'_ j \to U'$ is finite, and $V_ i' \cap V_ j'$ is (open and) closed both in $V'_ i$ and $V'_ j$. Hence $V_ i' \cap V_ j'$ is affine, and the map

\[ \mathcal{O}(V'_ i) \otimes _{\mathbf{Z}} \mathcal{O}(V'_ j) \longrightarrow \mathcal{O}(V'_ i \cap V'_ j) \]

is surjective. This implies that $Y'$ is separated, see Schemes, Lemma 26.21.7. Finally, consider the commutative diagram

\[ \xymatrix{ \coprod _{j = 1, \ldots , m} V'_ j \ar[rd] \ar[rr] & & Y' \ar[ld] \\ & U' & } \]

The south-east arrow is finite, hence proper, the horizontal arrow is surjective, and the south-west arrow is separated. Hence by Morphisms, Lemma 29.42.9 we conclude that $Y' \to U'$ is proper. Since it is also quasi-finite, we see that it is finite by Lemma 37.44.1, and we win. $\square$

Lemma 37.44.2. Let $f : X \to S$ be a morphism of schemes. Let $s \in S$. Assume that $f$ is proper and $f^{-1}(\{ s\} )$ is a finite set. Then there exists an open neighbourhood $V \subset S$ of $s$ such that $f|_{f^{-1}(V)} : f^{-1}(V) \to V$ is finite.

Proof. The morphism $f$ is quasi-finite at all the points of $f^{-1}(\{ s\} )$ by Morphisms, Lemma 29.21.7. By Morphisms, Lemma 29.57.2 the set of points at which $f$ is quasi-finite is an open $U \subset X$. Let $Z = X \setminus U$. Then $s \not\in f(Z)$. Since $f$ is proper the set $f(Z) \subset S$ is closed. Choose any open neighbourhood $V \subset S$ of $s$ with $f(Z) \cap V = \emptyset $. Then $f^{-1}(V) \to V$ is locally quasi-finite and proper. Hence it is quasi-finite (Morphisms, Lemma 29.21.9), hence has finite fibres (Morphisms, Lemma 29.21.10), hence is finite by Lemma 37.44.1. $\square$

Lemma 30.21.1. (For a more general version see More on Morphisms, Lemma 37.44.1.) Let $f : X \to S$ be a morphism of schemes. Assume $S$ is locally Noetherian. The following are equivalent

  1. $f$ is finite, and

  2. $f$ is proper with finite fibres.

Proof. A finite morphism is proper according to Morphisms, Lemma 29.45.11. A finite morphism is quasi-finite according to Morphisms, Lemma 29.45.10. A quasi-finite morphism has finite fibres, see Morphisms, Lemma 29.21.10. Hence a finite morphism is proper and has finite fibres.

Assume $f$ is proper with finite fibres. We want to show $f$ is finite. In fact it suffices to prove $f$ is affine. Namely, if $f$ is affine, then it follows that $f$ is integral by Morphisms, Lemma 29.45.7 whereupon it follows from Morphisms, Lemma 29.45.4 that $f$ is finite.

To show that $f$ is affine we may assume that $S$ is affine, and our goal is to show that $X$ is affine too. Since $f$ is proper we see that $X$ is separated and quasi-compact.
